JCAP Pre-Proposal Form Revised 2021 Joint Committee on Academic Planning Pre-Proposal for New Programs Part I: Title and affiliation(s) of proposed program: Program Title: World Language Education Program Degree Type: B.A.
Proposer(s): Iñaki Pérez Ibáñez, Assistant Professor in Spanish and Teacher Education Department(s): School of Education College(s): College of Education and Professional Studies Part II.
Briefly provide the following information (not to exceed two pages): The School of Education currently offers a Bachelor of Arts degree in Secondary Education, with multiple tracks reflecting various specializations.
Since its inception, the World Language Education Program has been one of these tracks (the other tracks are English, History/Social Studies, Mathematics, and Science).
Upon graduation, students in the Secondary Education Program obtain certification to teach at the High School level (grades 7-12).

Upon the completion of an additional course and a teach ing practicum at a Middle School, students in this existing program also have the option to obtain a Middle School extension, a credential that allows them to teach in grades 5-8 in any Rhode Island elementary, middle, or junior high school.
Recently the Rhode Island Department of Education changed the World Language teacher certification system.
Due to these changes, graduates from our current Secondary Education – World Language program are now certified to teach in Rhode Island at all levels of elementary, middle, and secondary education (grades PK-12).
The new program proposal is intended address the changes in Rhode Island certification regulations, which will require significant changes (over 25%) to the requirements for our current BA in Secondary Education with a specialization in World Languages, effectively transforming it into a BA in World Language Education -All Grades.

In the proposed new program, students will take a variety of existing EDC courses in Elementary Education, Early Childhood Education, Secondary Education, and Teaching English as a Second Language / Bilingual Education concentrations so that, upon graduation, they will be more versatile and highly employable educators who are better prepared to teach effectively in a wider variety of educational settings.
The financial cost to the university of this new program will be zero, as our students will be required to take existing courses that are regularly offered in the School o f Education.
The development of new courses will not be necessary to implement the proposed overhaul of the program.
The new program will not require the hiring of any new faculty (neither full time nor adjunct faculty).

JCAP Pre-Proposal Form Revised 2021 One of the purposes of the new program is to attract, retain, and graduate more teachers from multicultural, multilingual, historically marginalized, and under-represented groups in the education profession.
The inclusion of coursework in Bilingual Education and Teaching English as a Second Language aims to attract and harness the unique talents and lived experiences of students from our important local and regional multilingual communities.
In addition to this, the RI Department of Education, through the work of the Rhode Island Council on Elementary and Secondary Education, is currently in the process of changing the state’s high school graduation requirements.
Among the proposed changes to the system, students will be required to take a minimum of two years of study of the same language in order to successfully graduate from high school.
This change has the potential to strengthen the general pipeline of candidates for our proposed World Langua ge Education-All Grades program.

Finally, given both the regional and national shortage of world language educators, as evidenced by the 100% employment rates of graduates from our existing program and the high percentage of new language teachers who are being hired through an emergency certification process, the demand for well-qualified K-12 world language educators is high and the urgent need for this program is clear.

5.10.10 Committees, Boards, Councils and other such entities which have a university-wide function are described in this chapter. With few exceptions, committees with a narrower scope are not included here. For information on them, consult policy documents of various campus units, such as college by-laws, where available, and the Graduate Student Manual. Standing committees of the Faculty Senate, although having university-wide function, can be found in the by-laws of the Faculty Senate.

5.10.11 The committees included here are organized according to the jurisdictional rubric under which they fall, and are divided into (1) committees falling under presidential jurisdiction; (2) committees falling under direct jurisdiction of the general faculty or of the Graduate Faculty; and (3) committees falling under the joint purview of the Faculty Senate and the President. The division into the various jurisdictional rubrics has been proposed by a Faculty Senate Constitution, By-Laws, and University Manual (CBUM) subcommittee on the basis of research conducted during the 2001-02 academic year. This research primarily took into consideration the jurisdictional divide between the President (administration) and the Faculty Senate resulting from Article II of the Senate Constitution; when this was not conclusive, the historic understanding of who had jurisdiction at the time of the establishment of a committee or its predecessor was taken into account. In most cases, these criteria allowed a clear determination of a committee’s jurisdictional rubric. To limit future disputes about jurisdiction, the subcommittee proposed that the Faculty Senate endorse and accept the jurisdictional division resulting from the subcommittee’s research, the senate did so at its meeting on November 11, 2003, and the President endorsed the senate legislation on December 5, 2003.

CASC Procedures

The Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) Procedures CASC examines course and program proposals to ensure they are comprehensible and user-friendly for undergraduate students.
Within the Kuali proposal, we examine all ﬁelds to conﬁrm clear details vital to student success, such as prerequisites, course rationale and description, the number of seats and sections offered per year, and syllabi.
Syllabi should accompany all major course proposals (new classes, signiﬁcant modiﬁcations to a course).
To ensure proposal syllabi will be clear to students, we look for: ● straight-forward course information (class description & objectives, method of instruction); ● clear course policies, structures, and methods of teaching; ● clarity regarding grade scale & methods, assignments, and how coursework connects to credit hours; ● current information about accessible technological resources and apps necessary for the class; Further, students are best served by having up-to-date information on support services such as DAI; illness policies; and procedures reﬂecting current University standards.
Where these items are overlooked or out-of-date, CASC may provide friendly feedback.

Also, ATL has resources and templates for syllabi ( https://web.uri.edu/atl/design/syllabus/ ).
New courses should provide supporting documentation uploaded by the chair of the department/academic unit into the proper Kuali ﬁeld, indicating the date that their department/program voted to approve the course.
Program-level proposals should include all materials relevant to the new program/proposed changes, including supporting documentation from other academic units impacted by these changes.
All program and applicable accreditation requirements should be listed .
The Kuali ﬁelds for program proposals should include courses impacted by changes.
Course and Program Overlap Overlap is when a newly proposed or modiﬁed course/program intersects with the content of an existing course or program.
The amount of overlap might range from small (the topics of a single class) to approaching virtual duplication.
Proposers and curriculum approval committees can use search features within Kuali to compare other current and proposed courses/programs for potential overlap.

When CASC recognizes potential overlap, they will ask the course proposer and department/instructor to consult regarding the degree and signiﬁcance of overlap.
Even with substantial replication in content, there might be key differences in approach.
As CASC cannot be experts in all disciplines, we request that the proposer and faculty for the existing course/program work together.
This collaboration can be documented in a statement communicating the resolution to CASC.
If this collaboration cannot occur, CASC exercises its best judgment regarding student beneﬁt.
Note: overlap issues can also be addressed on the Faculty Senate ﬂoor or even at ﬁnal approval with the President.
We also encourage colleges to check for overlap themselves.
Starting in Fall 2025, CASC’s ‘Proposed Temporary and Permanent Courses/Programs’ email will be distributed at the end of the last full week of each month.
We encourage each college’s curriculum committee to meet during the ﬁrst full week of each month and, as part of their deliberations, carefully consider all newly proposed offerings in that CASC newsletter for potential overlap.

Course Approval Process

The Course/Program Approval Process at URI 1.
Initial Submission on Kuali.
Faculty members submit course (for both new and modified classes) and program proposals within Kuali Curriculum Management.
Kuali provides workflow at URI for curricular changes and is in the university’s Microsoft 365 suite; further information and login link can be found here: https://web.uri.edu/facsen/kuali/.
A library impact statement will be generated for new courses within one week of submission to Kuali.
Crosslisted classes, courses/programs that might overlap with existing offerings, and classes/programs assuming prerequisites from other departments need to provide documentation regarding approval from those other relevant academic units.
New programs need to allow two weeks for a Budget Impact Statement to be completed by the Budget Office.
Note: new programs must also complete the New Program Assessment Plan (https://web.uri.edu/atl/assessment/newprograms/) and submit it to the Assessment Team at assess@uri.edu. 2.
Approval Requirements.

Once a faculty member submits a new course proposal, either the department’s curriculum committee or the department chair/program head must approve it based on the governance structure of the department.
This approval requires a vote of the faculty of the originating department.
Courses not originating within a specific department or college must be approved by the governing committee responsible for administering the program.
As part of their approval, the departmental curriculum committee or chairs/program heads must submit an official statement confirming departmental approval via faculty vote for the proposal. 3.
College-level Review.
After approval by the department, the proposal is reviewed for approval by the college curriculum committee(s), and then approved by the college dean or delegate.
Colleges assess course proposals for issues such as staffing, intra-college departmental and interdepartmental overlap, and collegewide programmatic needs and requirements. 4.
Senate Committee Review.
After college-level approval, proposals go to the Faculty Senate Specialist who formats and prepares them for the following month’s curriculum committee meetings.

Course/program proposals are directed to the appropriate Senate Committee(s): undergraduate General Education courses to the General Education Committee (GEC); all other undergraduate courses/programs to the Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC); graduate courses/programs to the Graduate Council (GC).
These committees examine proposals with an eye to legibility and benefit to students. 5.
Full Senate Review.
The GEC, CASC, and the GC each make monthly reports to the entire Faculty Senate.
During these reports, they bring forward all new course/program proposals approved at the committee-level for a vote by the entire Senate.
Courses approved by this vote are then added to a bill for signature by the Faculty Senate President.
The President/Provost then provides final signature approval.
Concerns covered at this level typically include unexpected impacts on other programs or lack of resources.
Please note: 400 level courses proposed for graduate credit need to be approved by both the undergraduate and graduate committees within the department and college; at the Faculty Senate level, these proposals go before both the GC and CASC.

Please also note: courses are not approved for an immediate change; after completion of the approval process, they only become active in the term and year indicated in the proposal.
A complete proposal approved by each of the necessary levels might move through the process in 2-3 months.
Faculty submitting course proposals should carefully consult the meeting schedules for their college-level curriculum committee(s); the GEC, CASC, and GC; and the Faculty Senate itself.
They should also watch for notifications from Kuali if one of these bodies needs more information.

We are at a unique moment in our history where long-standing struggles of racism, gender inequality, LGBTQ+, socio-economic status, ability, and religious differences are intensified and up for debate in the public and private spheres.
Knowing more about the root causes of the struggles LGBTQ+ individuals experience in the areas of employment, housing, politics, immigration controls, and legal institutions, to name a few, creates an opening for students to engage in systemic change and re-think their lived experiences.
The purpose of this minor is to expose students to histories, theories, concepts, and methods that have contested historical and ongoing harm and oppression.
Students are encouraged to examine their social location, lived experiences, collaborative engagement, and organizing capacity to transform our world by learning how societal structures keep inequality and oppression alive.
The QTS Minor will offer students, especially younger generations, an opportunity to read, discuss, and engage with transnational issues that affect the lives of queer and transgender communities.

Since we live in a transnational world, the QTS minor will allow students to read, think, and analyze social justice issues through an interdisciplinary and intersectional framework.
While the QTS is complementary and overlaps with courses in the GWS, this minor offers an advanced level of proficiency in Queer and Transgender studies, politics, and culture, with a social justice commitment to scholarship, community engagement, and global citizenship.
From participating in interdisciplinary and innovative research, to social activism, to policy work in housing, wage gap, mental and medical services, media coverage, and decriminalization, these are some of the issues in which students will gain exposure, knowledge, and practical experiences to the problems affecting queer and transgender communities.
By broadening the scope of the QTS minor through an interdisciplinary and intersectional framework, students will be able to expand their prospects in the job market.

Program Educational Objectives.

Three to �ve years after graduation from the B.S. in Computer Engineering, graduates will: 1) Successfully practice computer engineering to serve state and regional industries, government agencies, or national and international industries. 2) Work professionally in one or more of the following areas: computer hardware and software design, embedded systems, computer networks and security, system integration, and electronic design automation. 3) Achieve personal and professional success with awareness and commitment to their ethical and social responsibilities, both as individuals and in team environments. 4) Maintain and improve their technical competence through lifelong learning, including entering and succeeding in an advanced degree program in a �eld such as engineering, science, or business.

Program Description.
Digital computer and communication systems have transformed society in a profound way.

The examples range from super powerful scienti�c computers, to embedded systems such as smart phones, internet of things (IoT), and smart cities.
Traditionally, computer engineering has been a discipline that combines both electrical engineering and computer science.
The URI computer engineering program is thus designed so the students will have a strong foundation in the relevant �elds of electrical engineering and computer science, while establishing themselves with the latest computer engineering topics, such as advanced computer architecture, computer network and cyber-physical security, big data learning and processing, and �eld programmable gate array (FPGA).
The computer engineering core courses can be categorized as follows: (1) ELE 208/209, 305, and 408/409 are core courses for computer system architecture and hardware and software organization and interaction. (2) ELE 201/202, 301/302, and 405/406 are the core courses for digital design with electronic design automation and rapid prototyping, and for computer system integration. (3) ELE 313 and 437 are core courses for computer communication and networks.

The computer engineering program has three professional electives in the senior year so students can further expand into areas such as signals and systems, digital control, electronics, and computer software.
The computer engineering program culminates in the senior year with two major design experiences.
ELE 408/409 is where all the skills accumulated through the curriculum will be employed in a group senior design project.
ELE 480 and 481 provide each student with the opportunity to work in a multi-disciplinary team in a senior capstone design project.
